rows.name: Bull Put Spread
rows.outlook: You expect the stock to stay above the higher strike through expiration.
rows.legs: Sell the higher-strike put and buy the lower-strike put in the same expiration, opening for a net credit.
rows.summary: A bull put spread is a defined-risk credit strategy: you keep the credit if the stock holds above your short strike, and the long put caps your loss if it doesn't.
rows.when: Chosen when mildly bullish or neutral, to be paid up front with a known worst case instead of the open-ended risk of a naked put.
rows.risk: Maximum loss is larger than the credit and occurs below the lower strike. Time decay helps; a sharp drop hurts.

rows.name: Bear Call Spread
rows.outlook: You expect the stock to stay below the lower strike through expiration.
rows.legs: Sell the lower-strike call and buy the higher-strike call in the same expiration, opening for a net credit.
rows.summary: A bear call spread is the bearish mirror of the bull put spread: a defined-risk credit position that profits when the stock stays below your short strike.
rows.when: Used when mildly bearish or neutral, to collect premium with a capped loss rather than shorting stock or selling a naked call.
rows.risk: Maximum loss (width minus credit) occurs above the higher strike. A strong rally is the risk.

rows.name: Bull Call Spread
rows.outlook: You expect the stock to rise toward or past the higher strike.
rows.legs: Buy the lower-strike call and sell the higher-strike call in the same expiration, paying a net debit that caps the upside.
rows.summary: A bull call spread is a defined-risk debit strategy for a bullish view — cheaper than an outright call, with profit capped at the higher strike.
rows.when: Chosen when bullish but wanting to spend less than an outright call and comfortable capping the gain.
rows.risk: Maximum loss is the debit paid, below the lower strike. Time decay works against you.

rows.name: Bear Put Spread
rows.outlook: You expect the stock to fall toward or past the lower strike.
rows.legs: Buy the higher-strike put and sell the lower-strike put in the same expiration, paying a net debit that caps the downside profit.
rows.summary: A bear put spread is a defined-risk debit strategy for a bearish view — cheaper than an outright put, with profit capped at the lower strike.
rows.when: Used when bearish but wanting to reduce the cost and time-decay drag of a long put.
rows.risk: Maximum loss is the debit paid, above the higher strike. The move must happen before expiration.

rows.name: Covered Call on High-Dividend Stocks
rows.outlook: You own the shares, are neutral-to-mildly-bullish, and want extra income on top of the dividend.
rows.legs: Hold 100 shares and sell one call against them. The call premium is income now; if the stock is called away you sell at the strike.
rows.summary: A covered call turns shares you already hold into an income position: you collect a premium, cap your upside at the strike, and keep any dividend paid before assignment.
rows.when: Income-focused holders pair covered calls with high-dividend, lower-volatility blue chips: the dividend plus the premium stack, and such names tend to grind rather than gap, so being capped hurts less. The trade-off is real — a takeover or a sharp rally leaves your gains capped at the strike.
rows.risk: The premium only cushions the first part of a decline; you still carry the stock's full downside below breakeven. Watch the ex-dividend date — a deep in-the-money call can be assigned early, costing you the dividend you sold it to keep.

rows.name: Cash-Secured Put on High-Volatility Stocks
rows.outlook: You would be happy to own the stock lower, and you set aside the cash to buy it.
rows.legs: Sell one put and hold strike x 100 in cash per contract. If assigned you buy the shares at the strike; if not, you keep the premium.
rows.summary: A cash-secured put pays you to wait for a price you'd buy at. Your effective purchase price, if assigned, is the strike minus the premium you collected.
rows.when: Higher-volatility names carry fatter premiums, so the income for standing ready to buy is larger — which is exactly why traders use cash-secured puts there. The flip side: higher volatility means a real chance you are assigned well above where the stock then trades.
rows.risk: Your downside is almost the same as owning the stock outright: if it falls hard you are assigned at the strike and ride it down from there, cushioned only by the premium. 'Cash-secured' means the cash is set aside, not that the trade is low-risk.

rows.name: Iron Condor on Index Options
rows.outlook: You expect the index to stay inside a range — neither a big rally nor a big drop.
rows.legs: Sell a put spread below the market and a call spread above it, both for credit. The two spreads define a range you want price to stay inside.
rows.summary: An iron condor is a defined-risk, range-bound credit strategy: you profit if the underlying finishes between your short strikes, and both wings cap your loss.
rows.when: Broad index options (like SPY or QQQ) are a common home for condors: they are diversified so they gap less than single stocks, and they are deeply liquid, which keeps the four legs' costs tight. Traders put them on when they expect calm and want to be paid for it.
rows.risk: Maximum loss is larger than the credit and happens if the index runs past either short strike. A condor is short volatility — a sharp move either way, or a volatility spike, works against you, and there are two sides that can be breached.

rows.name: Long Straddle for Biotech Catalysts
rows.outlook: You expect a large move but not the direction — typical around a binary event.
rows.legs: Buy a call and a put at the same strike and expiration. You pay for both, so the position starts at a loss and needs a move to pay off.
rows.summary: A long straddle is a bet on a big move in either direction. You buy a call and a put at the same strike; your loss is capped at what you paid, and you profit only if the stock moves far enough past either breakeven.
rows.when: Traders use straddles ahead of binary events such as a biotech FDA decision, where the outcome can gap the stock sharply up or down. The catch is that options are priced for that uncertainty — implied volatility is high going in, so you pay up, and if the move is smaller than priced, or the decision slips, the position loses value.
rows.risk: Maximum loss is the full premium paid, realized if the stock sits near the strike at expiration. High implied volatility before the event means you're paying up; a muted reaction or a delay works against you quickly.

rows.name: Long Strangle for Macro Rate Decisions
rows.outlook: You expect a large move but not the direction, and want a cheaper entry than a straddle.
rows.legs: Buy an out-of-the-money call and an out-of-the-money put. Both cost less than at-the-money options, so the entry is cheaper — but the underlying has to travel further to pay off.
rows.summary: A long strangle is a lower-cost cousin of the straddle: you buy an OTM call and an OTM put, pay less, and need a bigger move to profit. Loss is capped at the premium paid.
rows.when: Used around macro events — an FOMC rate decision or a major data release — that can reprice a whole index. The lower entry cost is the appeal; the trade-off is wider breakevens, so a moderate move can still lose.
rows.risk: Maximum loss is the premium paid, in the zone between the two strikes. Because both options start out-of-the-money, a move that isn't big enough leaves both worthless.

rows.name: Protective Collar for Unrealized Gains
rows.outlook: You hold a stock that has risen, want to protect the gain, and will accept a capped upside to pay for it.
rows.legs: Own the shares, buy a protective put below the price for a floor, and sell a call above the price whose premium pays for the put — often a 'zero-cost collar.'
rows.summary: A protective collar brackets a stock you own: a bought put sets a floor you can't fall below, and a sold call caps your upside and pays for the put. It locks a range around an unrealized gain without selling the shares.
rows.when: Long-term holders use collars to defend a large unrealized gain through an uncertain stretch without triggering a taxable sale. The cost is your upside — if the stock keeps running, you're capped at the call strike.
rows.risk: Below the put strike you're protected, but the cap means you forgo gains above the call strike, and a sold call can be assigned early, costing an upcoming dividend. 'Zero-cost' refers to the option premiums netting out, not to giving up nothing — you're trading away upside.

educational.name: The Wheel Strategy
educational.outlook: A repeatable income loop on a stock you are willing to own.
educational.summary: The Wheel is not a single trade with one payoff — it is a loop. You sell cash-secured puts on a stock you'd be happy to own; if you're assigned, you then sell covered calls against those shares; if they're called away, you start again selling puts.
steps: Sell a cash-secured put on a stock you want to own at the strike. Collect the premium.
If the put expires worthless, keep the premium and repeat. If you're assigned, you now own the shares at an effective price of strike minus premium.
Sell a covered call against the shares you now hold. Collect that premium too.
If the call expires worthless, keep the premium and sell another. If the shares are called away, you've sold at the strike — go back to step one.
educational.when: Income traders run the Wheel on blue-chip names they genuinely want to hold, because every step assumes you may end up owning the stock. It stacks put and call premiums over time.
educational.risk: You carry full ownership risk whenever you hold the shares: a serious decline in the underlying is the Wheel's real danger, and no amount of premium fully offsets it. Only run it on stock you'd be comfortable owning through a drawdown.
